summary:
Ucayali stands under the national framework of Peru, which does not criminalise trans identity but has legislated in 2025 against trans people's use of public facilities matching their gender identity. On 2 April 2025 the congressional Plenary approved and exempted from a second vote a law whose article 5 bars any person from entering or using a public sanitary service that does not correspond to their 'biological sex', with narrow exceptions for custody situations, places where medical attention is required, and accompanying an elderly person, a child under 12 or a person with disabilities. The same package bans 'ambiguous' bathroom signage, including inclusive wording such as 'women in their diversity', and its vague child-protection articles enable censorship of identity, artistic and educational content.

The legislative origin of that restriction is traceable. On 20 February 2025 the congressional Women and Family Commission unanimously approved a dictamen merging bills 6506 and 8457, introduced by Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Muñante, and the measure passed the plenary in April 2025. A July 2023 social-media complaint over the gendered restroom labels at Jorge Chávez International Airport in Lima set the process in motion. LGTBIQ activist Gianna Camacho warned at the time that restroom access would come to depend on the personal judgement of security staff, including identity-document checks, and noted that there is no record of sexual assault by trans women in women's restrooms. The Pontifical Catholic University of Peru's human-rights institute IDEHPUCP concludes that article 5 violates the equal-treatment and non-discrimination principle of article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights, and that the law rests on a stigmatising stereotype presenting trans people as likely restroom harassers when UN reporting shows trans people are more often victims than aggressors.

Hate-crime protection for LGBT people is absent from Peru's law. Congress voted in 2017 to strip LGBT protections from the new Penal Code's hate-crime provisions, with Popular Force and Alliance for Progress members carrying the repeal after an April Constitutional Committee vote and amid a petition claiming one million signatures. That outcome left Peru one of only three South American countries, alongside Paraguay and Guyana, without LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in its hate-crime law.

Violence against trans people is documented and, according to its own researchers, under-recorded. A 2024 report found hate crimes rising in Peru with trans women most affected; its co-author, trans journalist and human-rights defender Gianna Camacho, stressed that the recorded figures are only a sub-registry. Between 2020 and 2023, 54 transgender and gender-diverse people were killed, trans women again the most affected group.

Enforcement reaches private as well as public life. A consumer-protection body dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against a gym that enforced the 2025 bathroom policy. On television, presenter Ana María Salcedo of Willax publicly harassed Susel Paredes, the first openly lesbian member of Congress, telling her to 'go use the men's room'; Congressman Lizarzaburu made dehumanising comparisons about trans people on the floor of Congress, a record captured by IDEHPUCP.

The Inter-American Court of Human Rights held in Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 that gender identity falls under protected personal autonomy and that states must guarantee trans people's full rights. In December 2025 three police officers, Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León, were sentenced to 17 years' imprisonment for the rape and torture of Azul Rojas Marín, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, nearly 20 years after the attack and after years of litigation. It was Peru's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and, per BBC News Mundo, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history; the case reached the Court through the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights.

A trans visitor to Ucayali should therefore expect to face the national restroom restriction as applied wherever security staff or building rules determine access, with no hate-crime coverage in the Penal Code to fall back on, and with official violence figures that are acknowledged to understate the problem.
tangentialFactors:
Two protective developments sit alongside the restrictions and do not undo them. In June 2024 Peru's health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, described as a step toward dignity for trans patients in healthcare settings. In July 2025 a Lima constitutional court, after an activist legal challenge, ruled an anti-equality decree unconstitutional. Neither development alters article 5 of the April 2025 law, which remains in force.

The April 2025 package carries a second, speech-facing dimension. Vague child-protection articles, including an article 4 ban on media and advertising content, enable censorship of identity, artistic and educational material, and the minimum sentence for obscenity was raised from three to four years. Human Rights Watch states that child protection is a pretext for repression and the scapegoating of trans people. The same package's restroom provisions were described by IDEHPUCP as legalized discrimination against trans access to public space.

The Inter-American framework provides a counterweight of its own. Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 obliges states to guarantee trans people's full rights on the basis of protected personal autonomy, and the Azul Rojas Marín judgment shows that the regional system can reach a state whose domestic enforcement failed for decades. The regional comparison is also relevant: Peru stands with Paraguay and Guyana as one of three South American countries without LGBT hate-crime coverage.
localsOnly:
Resident-facing, the record for Ucayali is thin at the subnational level. No source in this inventory records a regional ordinance, an incident series, a facility rule or an enforcement pattern specific to Ucayali; the binding text is national, and the practical question for residents is how security staff and building administrators apply article 5 to regional public facilities.

The evidence that exists about everyday enforcement is drawn from elsewhere in Peru and is consistent with the national pattern. A consumer-protection body dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against a gym that enforced the policy, which suggests that complaints about access restrictions are unlikely to succeed through that channel. Activists and researchers warn that restroom access will turn on the personal judgement of security staff, including identity-document checks, and that no record supports the premise that trans women have assaulted anyone in women's restrooms.

Civil society and academic institutions carry much of the documentation. IDEHPUCP, based at the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru, published the legal analysis of article 5 by Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte, and documented the dehumanising floor remarks of Congressman Lizarzaburu. Gianna Camacho, a trans journalist and human-rights defender, co-authored the 2024 report on rising hate crimes and stressed that the published figures are only a sub-registry, meaning residents in Ucayali should not read the absence of local records as the absence of local incidents.

Two state actions have been favourable to trans residents: the June 2024 removal of pathologising gender-diversity terminology from official health guidance, and the July 2025 ruling of a Lima constitutional court striking down an anti-equality decree after an activist challenge. Both were obtained outside the legislative process and neither has been shown to have been implemented regionally.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory reports Ucayali-specific legal, enforcement, incident or health-system findings on trans people. The absence of regional records is a gap in the evidence, not a finding that conditions in Ucayali are benign or that none exist; the regional violence data cited here are national and were described by their own co-author as a sub-registry.

Whether article 5 of the April 2025 law has been enforced at particular Ucayali public facilities, and how security staff apply the exceptions for custody, medical attention or accompanying children, elderly or disabled people, are unresolved on this evidence. Likewise unsourced is whether the June 2024 health guidance has been implemented in Ucayali health facilities, whether the July 2025 Lima constitutional ruling has been applied regionally, and how the raised obscenity sentence and article 4 media ban are being used against identity-related content in the region.

The inventory does not document trans-specific violence in Ucayali, any regional hate-crime statistics, or any marker or document-change procedure specific to Peru beyond the general absence of criminalisation; no Peruvian law identified here regulates gender-marker changes on identity documents. The July 2023 bathroom-label complaint that triggered the 2025 legislation concerned Jorge Chávez International Airport in Lima, and the sources do not establish how far the resulting restriction reaches private premises such as hotels, shopping centres and workplaces in Ucayali.
